description: Evaluation cases for the https-outcalls skill. Tests whether agents use the correct 2MB response limit (2,000,000 bytes per the interface spec, not 2^21), the correct cycle cost for omitting max_response_bytes on a 13-node subnet, that the Application-subnet cost formula does not apply on a cloud engine, that max_response_bytes covers header bytes and bounds the transform's output, that over-attaching cycles costs outcall concurrency, and that an outcall has two distinct timeouts with different reject codes rather than one that traps.

output_evals.name: 2MB limit is 2,000,000 bytes and the default-size cost
output_evals.prompt: For an IC HTTPS outcall: what is the exact maximum value in bytes I can pass for max_response_bytes, and under the legacy version 1 pricing that is still the replica default, roughly how many cycles does a 13-node subnet charge if I leave max_response_bytes unset? Just the two numbers with a one-line justification each.
expected_behaviors: States the maximum as 2,000,000 bytes (decimal), NOT 2_097_152 / 2^21 / 2 MiB
Gives the omitted-max_response_bytes cost as roughly 20.8-20.9 billion cycles
Does NOT state the cost as ~21.5 billion or ~21.86 billion cycles

output_evals.name: Adversarial: outcall cycle cost on a cloud engine
output_evals.prompt: My canister runs on a cloud engine (a CloudEngine subnet) and makes an HTTPS outcall with the standard Call.httpRequest wrapper. Roughly how many cycles should I budget for this outcall, and do I need to attach any? Answer briefly.
expected_behaviors: States the cost is 0 on a cloud engine, not the ~20.8 billion Application-subnet figure
Says no cycles need to be attached and the standard wrapper already handles this correctly
Does NOT instruct topping up the canister with cycles or attaching a hardcoded non-zero fee

output_evals.name: Adversarial: max_response_bytes covers headers and bounds the transform output
output_evals.prompt: My IC canister calls a REST API whose JSON body is about 800 bytes. I planned to set max_response_bytes to 1024 and strip all response headers in my transform function to stay under it. Will that work? A few sentences, no code.
expected_behaviors: States that max_response_bytes covers HTTP header names and values plus the body, not the body alone
States that stripping headers in the transform will NOT rescue this request, because the raw response is checked against the cap before the transform runs
Also notes that max_response_bytes separately bounds the transform's own output, so the cap is enforced twice rather than only on the raw response
Advises sizing the cap against headers + body as received from the server (real APIs often send 1-2 KB of headers), so 1024 is too tight
Does NOT claim the 1024-byte cap will work because the transform removes the headers

output_evals.name: Adversarial: over-attaching cycles, and why version 2 changes the answer
output_evals.prompt: My IC canister makes one HTTPS outcall per user action. The computed cost is about 200M cycles. Since unused cycles are refunded, should I just attach 1B to be safe? A few sentences, no code. Say whether your answer depends on the pricing version.
expected_behaviors: Confirms unused cycles are refunded but states that over-attaching is still not free
Explains that attached cycles are held for the duration of the call, so a margin reduces how many outcalls can be in flight (caps concurrency)
States that the answer DOES depend on the pricing version

For version 2, explains that the attachment beyond the base fee becomes the per-node allowance, which sets the node's response deadline and transform instruction limit, so a larger attachment lets the call consume more and can therefore be CHARGED more

Recommends attaching the computed amount via the wrapper rather than a hand-picked buffer: Rust HttpRequest::send() (ic-cdk-management-canister 0.2) or Motoko Call.httpRequest, or cost_http_request / cost_http_request_v2 directly
Does NOT endorse attaching the 1B round number as a harmless safety margin
Does NOT name ic_cdk::management_canister::http_request, which ic-cdk 0.20 removed

output_evals.name: Adversarial: 'Http body exceeds size limit' fires on a body well under the cap
output_evals.prompt: My IC canister's HTTPS outcall fails with: Http body exceeds size limit of 10000 bytes. But the JSON body the API returns is only about 3 KB, well under 10000. What is going on? A few sentences, no code.
expected_behaviors: Explains that response header bytes are subtracted from max_response_bytes first, so the body was measured against the remaining allowance, not the full 10000
Notes the message prints the full cap rather than the remaining allowance, which is why a 3 KB body can trip a 10000-byte cap
Recommends raising max_response_bytes to cover headers plus body
Does NOT suggest that stripping headers in the transform function will fix this error

output_evals.name: Adversarial: two distinct outcall timeouts, neither of which traps
output_evals.prompt: My IC canister makes an HTTPS outcall to a third-party API that is sometimes very slow. What timeouts apply to the outcall, and what does my canister see when one is hit? A few sentences, no code.
expected_behaviors: Identifies TWO distinct timeouts: about 30 seconds for the remote server to respond, and 60 seconds for the subnet to produce a response
Pairs each with the right reject: SysFatal with message 'Timeout expired' for the 30s remote-server timeout, and SysTransient with message 'Canister http request timed out' for the 60s subnet timeout
States the call is rejected rather than trapped, so it is catchable (in Motoko the await raises an Error, in Rust the wrapper returns Err)
Does NOT claim there is a single ~30 second timeout, and does NOT claim the call traps

output_evals.name: Adversarial: the four version 2 expectations fund one pooled budget
output_evals.prompt: I set with_expected_roundtrip_time_ms(300) on a version 2 HTTPS outcall from my Rust canister. Does that mean the nodes will give up after 300ms if the server is slow? Explain what that value actually controls.
expected_behaviors: States that it does NOT impose a 300ms deadline on the request
Explains that the four expectations only decide how many cycles are attached, and are never sent to the replica

Explains that the attachment minus the base fee becomes a per-node allowance, and the deadline is derived from that whole remaining allowance at the per-millisecond price, so it lands far above the declared value
Does NOT claim the expectations are four independent per-dimension limits

output_evals.name: Adversarial: an under-funded version 2 outcall is accepted, not rejected
output_evals.prompt: If I attach fewer cycles than a pricing-version-2 HTTPS outcall needs, do I get an error immediately when I make the call? What happens?
expected_behaviors: States the up-front check is against the BASE FEE only, so the call is accepted rather than rejected
States it then runs with tighter per-node limits and can fail partway, possibly after the remote server was already contacted
Notes the failure is intermittent, depending on how slow the endpoint was and how much work the transform did

Mentions at least one of: CanisterReject 'Insufficient cycles' from a node exhausting its allowance, CanisterReject 'Out of cycles: ...' for a pooled shortfall, or the SysTransient no-consensus divergence
Does NOT claim the call is rejected up front the way an under-funded version 1 call is

output_evals.name: Adversarial: version 1 is unreachable through ic-cdk-management-canister 0.2
output_evals.prompt: My Rust canister uses ic-cdk-management-canister 0.2. How do I make an HTTPS outcall with pricing_version set to 1?
expected_behaviors: States that you cannot: the HttpRequest builder always sets pricing_version = 2 and there is no opt-out, and from_args overwrites the field
States that 0.2.0 removed the free http_request function, so the builder is the only path in that crate
Offers a correct escape hatch: pin ic-cdk-management-canister 0.1, or call aaaaa-aa directly and price with ic_cdk::api::cost_http_request
Does NOT invent a with_pricing_version setter or suggest setting the field on the args and passing them to the builder

output_evals.name: Adversarial: Motoko has no pay-as-you-go pricing yet
output_evals.prompt: Show me how to make a pay-as-you-go (pricing version 2) HTTPS outcall from a Motoko canister using the ic mops package.
expected_behaviors: States that Motoko has no version 2 path today: the published ic package (4.x) prices version 1 via Call.httpRequest
Does NOT fabricate a Motoko builder, a costHttpRequestV2 call, or a Cost.httpRequestV2 function as if it were available
Notes that ic 4.x's HttpRequestArgs has no pricing_version field at all, so a Motoko caller cannot set it and the call is version 1 by omission, consistently funded by the version 1 cost function
May note that Motoko support is planned but unreleased, and depends on a moc release

output_evals.name: Adversarial: pricing_version and the attached amount must agree
output_evals.prompt: My Rust canister sets pricing_version = 2 on an HTTPS outcall but attaches the amount from ic_cdk::api::cost_http_request. Is that a problem, and what would I see?
expected_behaviors: Identifies the mismatch: version 2 is in force but the attachment was computed with the version 1 cost function
States the call is ACCEPTED rather than rejected, because the up-front check is only the base fee
States it then runs on a smaller per-node allowance than version 2 intended, and can fail partway with tighter limits
Recommends letting one wrapper own both, e.g. HttpRequest::send() which pairs version 2 with cost_http_request_v2
Does NOT claim the replica rejects a version 2 call for an under-sized attachment up front
Does NOT claim pricing_version = 2 is unsupported or silently downgraded on current replicas

output_evals.name: Adversarial: flexible outcall committee size and variable response count
output_evals.prompt: Write the replication counts for a flexible_http_request that asks 5 nodes and returns once a majority answer, and tell me what my canister has to handle in the success case.
expected_behaviors: Derives total_requests from subnet_self_node_count() rather than hardcoding 5, noting total_requests must not exceed the subnet size
Gives min_responses as a strict majority of the committee (e.g. total_requests / 2 + 1)
States the canister must handle ANY count between min_responses and max_responses, and that fewer than max_responses is a normal success
States that responses are an unordered multiset that does not identify the producing node, and that each response's status must be checked separately
Does NOT claim the result arrives as a reject on failure: both arms of FlexibleHttpRequestResult are delivered as a reply

output_evals.name: Adversarial: why a default version 2 outcall reserves billions of cycles
output_evals.prompt: My Rust version 2 HTTPS outcall has max_response_bytes of 4000 and a transform that just clears headers, but it attaches over 5 billion cycles. Why, and what do I change?
expected_behaviors: Identifies the unset with_expected_transform_instructions defaulting to the 5,000,000,000 query instruction limit as almost the entire reservation
States that unset expectations reserve the maximum, including a 60-second round trip
Recommends declaring with_expected_transform_instructions and with_expected_roundtrip_time_ms, which brings it to roughly 112 million
Notes that for a call completing within either reservation the CHARGE does not change, only the cycles held during the call, so this is about outcalls in flight rather than the bill
Does NOT recommend lowering max_response_bytes as the primary fix, and does NOT recommend attaching a hand-picked smaller number

trigger_evals.description: Queries to test whether the skill activates correctly. 'should_trigger' queries should cause the skill to load; 'should_not_trigger' queries should NOT activate this skill.
should_trigger: My canister needs to fetch a price from a REST API
Why does my canister's outcall fail consensus with different responses per replica?
How much does it cost in cycles to call an external HTTPS endpoint from a canister?
How do I use flexible_http_request so each node returns its own response?
Should I set pricing_version 2 on my canister's HTTPS outcalls?
What do the with_expected_* setters on the Rust HttpRequest builder do?
should_not_trigger: How do I read an Ethereum contract's state from my canister?
